#Part 1
1.Open the sleep dataset in R 
```{r}
library(tidyverse)
data(sleep)
```

2. Is it long or wide format? How do you know? 
It is long. The same ID appears twice in the ID column, once for each group. So, we can infer that there is one row for each observation of the variable.

3. Transform this data so that it is in the other format. 
```{r}
sleep_wide <- pivot_wider(sleep, id_cols = "ID", names_from = "group", values_from = "extra", names_prefix = "drug")
```
I followed your format for the first few, in the later questions I used pipes and tidyverse style.

4. Transform your data back to its original format. 
```{r}
sleep_long <- pivot_longer(sleep_wide, cols = c("drug1", "drug2"), names_to = "group", names_prefix = "drug", values_to = "extra")
```

5. Open the Starwars dataset
```{r}
data("starwars")
```

6. Create homeworld as a factor. How many levels does it have? 
```{r}
homeworld_factor <- as.factor(starwars$homeworld)
nlevels(homeworld_factor)
```
There are 48 levels in homeworld_factor

7. Reorder homeworld so that Naboo is the reference group. 
```{r}
starwars$homeworld <- as.factor(starwars$homeworld)
starwars$homeworld <- relevel(starwars$homeworld, ref = "Naboo")
```

8. Use mutate to create a column transforming kg to pounds. (hint: you may need to look up the conversion)
```{r}
starwars <- starwars %>% 
  mutate(mass_lbs = mass * 2.20462)
```
mutate() creates the new column within the function

9. Print a summary of your column from #8
```{r}
summary(starwars$mass_lbs)
```

#Part 2
10. open the billboard dataset.
```{r}
data("billboard")
```

11. are the data in this dataframe in long or wide format? explain how you know. 
The billboard dataset is wide. There is one row per song and there are different columns for each 'observation' of the variable (position on the billboard 100).

12. change the data from its original format to the other version. 
```{r}
billboard_long <- pivot_longer(billboard, cols = starts_with("wk"), names_to = "week", names_prefix = "wk", values_to = "rank", values_drop_na = TRUE)
```
Could also use a pipe, but I matched the notes in the earlier examples.
```{r}
billboard %>% 
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("wk"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "wk",
    values_to = "rank",
    values_drop_na = TRUE
  )
```
starts_with() selects the columns without manually typing each one since they have a common prefix. names_prefix in pivot_longer() has the opposite use as in pivot_wider() and removes the "wk" from each entry in week. The answer to this is in the examples of the help file for pivot_longer().

13. change it from your altered version in #3 back to its original state. 
```{r}
billboard_wide <- billboard_long %>% 
  pivot_wider(
    id_cols = c(artist, track, date.entered),
    names_from = week,
    names_prefix = "wk",
    values_from = rank
  )
```
I'm assuming the numbering is off and you wanted me to change #12 back. I used a pipe for this one, I think I prefer the structure to the notes version, but I'm not sure if there is a functional difference? I noticed that I lost some variables because of values_drop_na above. I also noticed that the arguments in pivot_wider() work without quotation marks, probably pivot_longer() too.

AW comment: sorry about that! Pipes are great- it's my preferred way to transform data as well. Can you say more about the dropped variables? drop na should remove empty rows, but shouldn't get rid of other data.  

14. Separate the date entered column into three columns: one for year, one for month, and one for day. 
```{r}
billboard_sep <- billboard %>% 
  separate(
    date.entered,
    into = c("year", "month", "day"),
    sep = "-"
  )
```
In the original billboard dataset, the date is YYYY-MM-DD separated by dashes. Tidyverse style guide says that pipes and arguments should be followed by a new line, so that's why it looks like that.
